text:
In late August 1854, cholera struck the crowded Soho district of London with terrifying speed. Within about ten days, more than five hundred people living close to Broad Street had died. Cholera is a disease that causes violent diarrhea and rapid loss of body fluid, and in those days it could kill a healthy adult within a day or two. London had suffered earlier epidemics, and almost everyone, including most doctors, believed the cause was "miasma," a poisonous foul air that rose from rotting waste and filthy ground.

John Snow, a respected physician who lived and worked nearby, doubted this theory. He had already pioneered the use of anaesthesia, and he was a man who preferred evidence to received opinion. During an earlier outbreak in 1848 and 1849 he had begun to suspect that cholera was carried in something people swallowed rather than something they breathed. His reasoning was simple. The illness attacked the gut first, so it seemed far more likely to enter through the mouth than through the lungs. In 1849 he had published a short pamphlet arguing that contaminated water might spread the disease, but few readers had been persuaded.

The Broad Street outbreak gave him a chance to test his idea on a small and well-defined area. At that time, nobody knew about germs in the modern sense, and the microscope had not yet revealed the tiny living organisms that actually cause cholera. Snow therefore had to work from patterns alone. He walked the streets of Soho, knocked on doors, and asked grieving families where they had obtained their drinking water. Many households had no running supply and relied on public street pumps, and the pump on Broad Street was especially popular because its water was thought to be unusually clear and pleasant.

As he gathered his information, Snow marked each death on a map of the neighbourhood. He drew a small bar at the address of every victim, so that the deaths stacked up like tiny black blocks along the streets. The pattern was striking, because the bars clustered thickly around the Broad Street pump and thinned out with distance. To a modern eye this is the most famous part of the story, although the map was only one piece of a larger argument, and Snow's careful questioning mattered just as much.

What made his case convincing were the exceptions, which at first seemed to contradict the pattern. A workhouse near the pump housed several hundred poor residents, yet very few of them died. Snow discovered that the workhouse had its own well, and so its inmates had no need to visit the pump. A brewery on the nearby street employed dozens of men, and none of them fell ill. The workers there were given an allowance of free beer, and the brewery also had its own well, so they rarely drank from the pump at all. In contrast, he found a woman in Hampstead, far from Soho, who died after drinking Broad Street water. Her son had been sending her bottles of it because she liked the taste, and a niece who drank from the same supply also fell ill.

By early September, Snow believed he had enough to act. On the evening of the seventh he went to the local Board of Guardians, the parish officials who governed the area, and presented his findings. He urged them to remove the pump handle so that nobody could draw water from it. The officials were skeptical of his theory, but the evidence was too troubling to ignore, and the handle was taken off the next day. The pump was silenced, and residents had to find their water elsewhere.

It is tempting to say that this single act ended the epidemic, but the truth is more complicated. The outbreak had already been declining before the handle was removed, partly because many frightened residents had fled the district and partly because so many of the most vulnerable people had already died. Snow himself acknowledged this in his later writing, and he did not claim the removal had stopped the disease by itself. What the episode really showed was how a careful investigator could connect scattered tragedies to a single shared source.

The final piece of the puzzle came from a local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, who had begun as a skeptic and ended as Snow's closest ally. Whitehead interviewed residents more thoroughly than Snow could, and he eventually traced the start of the outbreak to a baby who had fallen sick with diarrhea in a house on Broad Street. The mother had washed the infant's soiled diapers, and the dirty water had been thrown into a cesspool that was found to be leaking close to the well. Upon inspection, the brick lining of the well was cracked, which allowed sewage to seep in and contaminate the water that so many people trusted.

Although official bodies initially rejected Snow's conclusions, his work slowly changed how people thought about disease and public health. He died in 1858, before his ideas were widely accepted. Within a few decades, however, scientists confirmed that germs in water cause cholera, and cities began building proper sewers and clean water supplies. Today Snow is remembered as a founder of epidemiology, the study of how diseases spread through populations, and his map remains a powerful reminder that patient observation can save lives.
